# Five tests {#sec-tests}

@sec-lrd ended with five calculations that would decide whether a fed quasi-star can be a Little Red Dot. This
chapter does them, each as far as the tools allow:

1. Electron scattering of the lines in the actual infall, by Monte Carlo (@sec-tests-es).
2. Infall at the equator with outflow at the poles (@sec-tests-axi).
3. The full Balmer series near the Balmer limit, for the break as observers measure it (@sec-tests-break).
4. A cooler quasi-star, run through TITAN and the non-LTE code like the first (@sec-tests-cool).
5. He I λ10830 and O I λ8446 (@sec-tests-metals).

None of them is a fit. They use the same TITAN run W30 and its non-LTE solution as the earlier chapters, except
test 4, which is a new run. Each section says what is computed and what is assumed. @sec-tests-summary collects
the results.

## Electron-scattering wings {#sec-tests-es}

**The calculation.** `julia/mc_escatter.jl` follows $10^6$ Hα photons through the infall of the non-LTE solution.

- *Emission.* Photons are emitted where the solution's net Sobolev line power is positive, in proportion to it. Their
  directions are weighted by the local escape probability, and their frequencies are the comoving line centre plus a
  thermal Doppler offset.
- *Thomson scattering.* Electrons have the solution's density and move with the infall plus a Maxwellian thermal
  velocity at the gas temperature. Scattering follows the dipole phase function with the first-order Doppler shift.
- *Line resonances.* Where a photon's comoving frequency crosses line centre, it is scattered again by the line with
  probability $1 - e^{-\tau(\mu)}$. There is no destruction, so this is an upper limit on line trapping.
- *Boundaries.* Photons that reach the star are absorbed; photons beyond the outer edge escape.

Without electrons, the code reproduces the ray-integrated profile of @sec-nlte to the level that its simplified
emission allows: FWHM 320 against 360 km s$^{-1}$, centroid −44 against −93 km s$^{-1}$ (`mc_validate.jl`)
**[tested]**.

| run | e⁻ scatterings per photon | FWHM [km s⁻¹] | centroid [km s⁻¹] | wing scale $W$ blue / red [km s⁻¹] | flux beyond −1000 / +1000 km s⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hα, no electrons | 0 | 340 | −44 | 151 / 359 | 0.001 / 0.006 |
| Hα, electrons at the gas temperature | 3.37 | 320 | −423 | 1023 / 333 | 0.171 / 0.007 |
| Hα, electrons at $10^4$ K (test) | 3.38 | 300 | −357 | 1278 / 583 | 0.195 / 0.046 |
| Hα, electrons at $3\times10^4$ K (test) | 3.37 | 300 | −236 | 1816 / 1107 | 0.205 / 0.111 |
| Hβ, electrons at the gas temperature | 6.71 | 480 | −891 | 1722 / 396 | 0.376 / 0.017 |

: Monte Carlo profiles of the escaping Hα and Hβ of the non-LTE solution of run W30. $W$: the e-folding velocity of
an exponential fitted to the profile between 600 and 2500 km s$^{-1}$ on each side (an exponential's FWHM is
$2\ln 2\,W = 1.39\,W$). Lines with "test" set every electron to the stated temperature **[computed]**.
{#tbl-tests-mc}

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="mc"></div>
```

**Result.** Electron scattering in the infall does make broad exponential wings: 17 % of the Hα flux ends up beyond
−1000 km s$^{-1}$, and the blue wing's e-folding velocity is 1020 km s$^{-1}$, an exponential FWHM of 1420 km s$^{-1}$.
That is the width @matthee2026 measures (1040–1600 km s$^{-1}$). The core keeps its width, about 320 km s$^{-1}$.

**But the wings are one-sided.** Almost all the broadening is to the blue. In a converging flow, each scattering
off an infalling electron shifts the photon, on average, to higher frequency, as in bulk Comptonization. Thermal
broadening is symmetric, and at the infall's 2000 K it is small. Hotter electrons (the test rows) symmetrize the wings
only partly. Even at $3\times10^4$ K the blue wing is 1.6 times wider than the red one **[computed]**. Hβ forms deeper,
scatters twice as often, and gets a blue wing 1.7 times as broad. Hα and Hβ therefore have different profiles, as in
the "Rosetta Stone" [@brazzini2025] **[computed; interpretation]**.

The observed wings are symmetric. Pure infall cannot make them; @sec-tests-axi shows what an outflow adds.

## Infall plus outflow {#sec-tests-axi}

**The model.** A star fed at the equator may lose gas at the poles. We have no two-dimensional hydrodynamics for this,
so we use a kinematic model on top of the spherical solution:

- inside two polar cones, $|\cos\theta| > \cos\theta_o$, the gas moves outwards at the local free-fall speed;
- elsewhere it falls in, as before;
- densities, level populations, line opacities and source functions are those of the spherical solution at the same
  radius.

In the Sobolev approximation the local line quantities depend on the flow only through $|dv/dr|$ and $v/r$, which
reversing the flow leaves unchanged. That the radiation field, and hence the source function, also stays the same is
an assumption. With it, $\theta_o = 0$ is the spherical infall and $\theta_o = 90°$ a spherical outflow.

The Monte Carlo of @sec-tests-es runs with the same cones (`theta=θ_o`), and `julia/axisym_lines.jl` integrates the
Hα and Hβ profiles along rays at inclinations $i$ (the angle between the line of sight and the outflow axis).

**Checks.** $\theta_o = 0$ reproduces the spherical Hα (peak 86 times the continuum, EW −810 Å against −805 Å in
@sec-nlte). $\theta_o = 90°$ gives its exact mirror image, as it must **[tested]**.

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="axisym"></div>
```

| $\theta_o$ | $i$ | Hα EW [Å] | Hβ EW [Å] | absorption trough against the star |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (infall) | — | −810 | −72 | redshifted, +175 km s$^{-1}$ (Hβ to 4 % of the continuum) |
| 30° | 0 | −425 | −62 | **blueshifted**, −175 km s$^{-1}$ |
| 30° | 45° | −642 | −62 | redshifted |
| 30° | 90° | −792 | −72 | redshifted |
| 60° | 0 | −724 | −70 | **blueshifted** |
| 60° | 45° | −442 | −48 | **blueshifted** (Hα too, to 0.87 of the continuum) |
| 60° | 90° | −622 | −68 | redshifted |
| 90 (outflow) | — | −810 | −72 | **blueshifted** |

: Hα and Hβ from the infall + outflow model of the W30 solution **[computed]**. {#tbl-tests-axi}

**What decides the sign of the absorber.** The gas that absorbs against the star is the gas on the line of sight to
it. Its velocity is set by whether that line of sight runs inside a cone. Looking down a cone ($i < \theta_o$), the
absorber flows out and is blueshifted; from the side, it falls in and is redshifted. A fraction $1 - \cos\theta_o$ of
observers look down a cone: 13 % for $\theta_o = 30°$, 50 % for $60°$ **[computed; the fraction is geometry]**. The
observed ratio, 38 of 46 Hα absorbers blueshifted and 10–15 % redshifted [@yanagisawa2026; @matthee2026], would
need outflow over most of the sky, $\theta_o \approx 80°$, with the inflow confined to a thin equatorial band
**[estimate]**. The redshifted minority, in the reddest, strongest-break sources, would then be the edge-on views.

**What it does to the wings.** In the Monte Carlo the asymmetry of the electron-scattering wings follows the balance
of the two flows. Pure outflow mirrors pure infall (centroid +423 km s$^{-1}$, red wing). With cones of
$\theta_o = 30°$ and $45°$ the profile is still blue-heavy (centroids −336 and −202 km s$^{-1}$; 15 % and 12 % of
the flux beyond −1000 km s$^{-1}$, against 2 % and 4 % beyond +1000 km s$^{-1}$). With $\theta_o = 60°$, where the two flows each fill half the sky, the wings become symmetric:
e-folding velocities 746 and 749 km s$^{-1}$, 7.8 % and 7.6 % of the flux beyond ∓1000 km s$^{-1}$, centroid
−7 km s$^{-1}$. The symmetry holds within 0.03 in these fractions at every inclination **[computed]**.

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="mcincl"></div>
```

**Caveats.**

- *The equivalent widths vary* from −425 to −810 Å with geometry. That comes from photons emitted in one flow being
  absorbed in the other at the same line-of-sight velocity, which the spherical source functions do not know about. The
  numbers are therefore indicative only.
- *The outflow is not a model.* It has the free-fall speed, the infall's density and its ionization. A real wind
  would be accelerated by radiation pressure on electrons at $L/L_{\rm Edd} \approx 1$, with its own density and
  temperature.

The test shows something narrower: a flow pattern that symmetrizes the wings also produces mostly blueshifted
absorbers. Whether a fed quasi-star drives such a flow is a question for two-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics
**[interpretation]**.

## The Balmer break as observers measure it {#sec-tests-break}

In @sec-lrd the break ratio $\langle f_\nu\rangle(4000$–4100 Å$)/\langle f_\nu\rangle(3620$–3720 Å$)$ came out at
1.35, although the continuum drops by a factor 5.5 at the edge. The blue window lies mostly redward of the 3646 Å
edge, where our spectrum had no lines above $n = 10$.

**The calculation.** `julia/balmer_series.jl` integrates rays through the infall with all Balmer lines from Hα to
$n = 40$ at once, their opacities and source functions added at every point, so that overlapping lines are treated
correctly. The wavelength grid runs from 3550 to 4150 Å in steps of 15 km s$^{-1}$, on top of the non-LTE continuum.

- *Populations.* Levels up to $n = 12$ come from the non-LTE solution. Higher levels take the departure coefficient
  of $n = 12$ (`bhigh=b12`) or LTE (`bhigh=lte`), which brackets them. They matter only for the line source
  functions; the opacity is set by $n = 2$.
- *Line profiles.* Gaussian, thermal plus 10 km s$^{-1}$ microturbulence, with no Stark broadening and no
  dissolution of high levels.
- *Resolution.* The spectrum is smoothed to resolving powers of 100 and 30, like a NIRSpec PRISM spectrum.

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="balmer"></div>
```

<!-- BALMER-TABLE -->

**Result.** The high Balmer lines, optically thick in the infall's $n = 2$ population, blanket the region just
redward of the edge. Between 3660 and 3700 Å the flux falls to 18–32 % of the continuum. The observers' break rises
from 1.27 to 3.6 with lines to $n = 40$ (3.4 at $R = 100$, 3.0 at $R = 30$) **[computed]**. Lines above $n = 40$
fall between the edge and 3656 Å. Even if that strip were black, the break could rise no further than 4.6, and to 4.3
if it is absorbed as deeply as the strip next to it (`balmer_bound.jl`) **[computed bound]**. A run with lines to
$n = 20$ gave 2.0, so the convergence in $n$ matters.

The model's break, 3.6–4.3, sits at the top of the range of most LRDs (none to about 3.5) and below the two extremes,
6.9 and 7.7 (@sec-lrd). The infall makes it, through the same $n = 2$ population that its far-UV pumping maintains.
The break is mostly not the jump in the continuum but the merging high series **[computed; interpretation]**.

## A cooler quasi-star {#sec-tests-cool}

**The run.** The star is the steady quasi-star of the same mass ($10^6\,M_\odot$) and luminosity
($1.42\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$), but with a black hole of $10^4$ instead of $10^5\,M_\odot$ ($f_{\rm BH} = 0.01$).
It is 1.6 times larger ($R = 1.35\times10^{16}$ cm) and cooler (5760 K). TITAN run C30 feeds it exactly like W30:
$3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ from $30R$, with the same grid and physics.

- *Length of the run.* It ran for $9.5\times10^7$ s, shorter than W30, because its time step collapsed to seconds near
  the end. Over the last $2\times10^7$ s the photosphere moved by less than $10^{-3}R$.
- *The fed photosphere.* $r_{\rm ph} = 0.977R$, $T_{\rm eff} \approx 5890$ K, $L \approx 1.04$ times the star's own
  luminosity **[computed]**.

The non-LTE calculation is the one of @sec-nlte, with one difference that matters.

- *No Unsöld–Lucy correction.* The C30 photosphere sits on the hydrogen recombination front, where the temperature
  falls from 12600 to 5900 K over three zones. There the continuum code's flux is 0.2–0.5 of TITAN's, and the
  correction diverged.
- *Energy is not conserved.* Without the correction, light that the infall sends back into the star is absorbed at
  fixed temperature. The emergent luminosity is $9.0\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, 59 % of TITAN's
  $1.52\times10^{44}$; the bare star alone already gives 88 %.
- *Consequence.* Absolute line luminosities below are therefore underestimates. Equivalent widths, ratios and the
  ionization structure are less affected. The ionization is cross-checked by the simple model, which uses the bare
  star's spectrum and has no such loss **[computed; caveat]**.

Convergence: 162 passes, the last ones changing populations by $< 4\times10^{-4}$ and the line power by 0.3 % over
ten passes.

**A much weaker far UV.** The far-UV excess that ionizes the W30 infall comes from the line-free zero-metal
photosphere (@sec-sm-mechanism). At 5890 K it is far smaller.

| $L_\nu/B_\nu(T_{\rm eff})$ at | 1000 Å | Lyα | 1500 Å | 4000 Å | 6563 Å |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| W30 star (7310 K) | 700 | 72 | 13 | 1.13 | 0.85 |
| C30 star (5890 K) | 224 | 5.4 | 0.3 | 1.28 | 0.97 |

: The stars' spectra relative to a blackbody at their effective temperature **[computed]**. {#tbl-tests-fuv}

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="cool"></div>
```

**The infall stays mostly neutral.**

| | W30 (7310 K) | C30 (5890 K) |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{\rm H}$ at about 4, 12 and 30 $R$ | 0.98 / 0.87 / 0.66 | 0.46 / 0.11 / 0.03 |
| neutral column [cm⁻²] | $8.5\times10^{23}$ | $3.2\times10^{24}$ |
| Thomson depth | 5.4 | 2.6 |
| Hα EW [Å] / $L$(Hα) [erg s⁻¹] | −805 / $9.0\times10^{42}$ | −164 / $1.6\times10^{42}$ |
| Hα absorption against the star | filled in | to 12 % of the continuum at +160 km s$^{-1}$ |
| Hβ EW [Å] | −73 | −15 (trough 3.5 % at +240 km s$^{-1}$) |
| Hα/Hβ | 5.3 | 7.9 |
| Paβ/Hα, Lyα/Hα | 0.12, 0.054 | 0.22, 0.022 |
| Balmer jump at the edge; break in the windows (continuum only) | 5.5; 1.35 | 4.6; 1.65 |
| $L_{\rm bol}/L({\rm H\alpha})$ | 15.5 | 58 (96 with TITAN's $L$) |
| τ_es outside the Hα-forming region (power-weighted) | 1.06 | 0.81 |

: The two fed quasi-stars with non-LTE hydrogen **[computed]**. Radii in units of each star's own $R$. The C30
luminosities are underestimates (see above). {#tbl-tests-cool}

**The simple model predicts it.** The closed formula of @sec-sm-closed, with the C30 star's spectrum and no fitting,
gives a neutral column of $3.08\times10^{24}$ cm$^{-2}$ against $3.07\times10^{24}$ in the full calculation, and a
Thomson depth of 2.38 against 2.41 on the same grid. The ionized fraction agrees to within 10 % out to $5R$, 15 % at $8R$,
and 45 % at worst beyond, where it is a few per cent. The far-UV pumping that the simple model isolates is what sets the ionization, in both stars
**[computed; tested]**.

**What changes against the LRDs.**

- *Closer to the data:* the photosphere (5890 K against ≈ 5000 K observed), the Balmer decrement (7.9, the median of
  @matthee2026), Paβ/Hα (0.22, against 0.35 in the Rosetta Stone), and a strong, redshifted Hα absorption trough, the
  "inflowing absorber" seen in the reddest LRDs [@matthee2026].
- *Further from the data:* Hα is five times weaker relative to the continuum. $L_{\rm bol}/L({\rm H\alpha})$ is 58
  even with the luminosity deficit (observed 11–30), and the Thomson-thick cocoon thins to 2.6.

Within this family of models, a cooler star trades Hα strength for a redder, more absorbed spectrum
**[computed; interpretation]**.

**Its wings.** The Monte Carlo of @sec-tests-es on the C30 solution gives 1.9 Thomson scatterings per Hα photon
(W30: 3.4) and the same one-sided wings: blue e-folding velocity 880 km s$^{-1}$, 13 % of the flux beyond
−1000 km s$^{-1}$, 1.4 % beyond +1000. With outflow cones of $\theta_o = 60°$ they become symmetric (649 and
654 km s$^{-1}$, 7 % on each side) **[computed]**. The thinner cocoon narrows the wings somewhat, but does not remove
them.

## Helium and oxygen {#sec-tests-metals}

### He I λ10830

**The calculation.** `julia/he10830.jl` computes the metastable 2³S population of helium in the infall. It uses a
three-state atom (1¹S, 2³S, He⁺) after @oklopcic2018, in the radiation field $J_\nu$ of the full non-LTE solution
(X-rays included) and at its temperatures and densities. The rates are approximate and stated in the code. The
λ10830 line is then computed along rays in the Sobolev approximation, with a pure-scattering source function.

| star, variant | 2³S column [cm⁻²] | λ10830 |
|---|---|---|
| W30 | $1.6\times10^{13}$ | emission, EW −9 Å |
| W30, recombination into 2³S × 3 | $4.9\times10^{13}$ | emission, EW −18 Å |
| W30, 2³S photoionization cross-section × 0.5 | $3.2\times10^{13}$ | emission, EW −14 Å |
| C30 (5890 K) | $3.7\times10^{14}$ | emission, EW −18 Å; a 3 % dip at +900 km s$^{-1}$ |

: He I 2³S columns (radial) and λ10830 for the two fed stars **[computed]**. {#tbl-tests-he}

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="tests" data-view="he"></div>
```

**Result.** The 2³S level is populated by recombination of He⁺, and there is almost no He⁺. The zero-metallicity
photosphere at 7300 K emits very few photons above 24.6 eV, and the shock's X-rays are absorbed close to it. The He⁺
fraction is 7 % at the base of the infall and $5\times10^{-6}$–$2\times10^{-4}$ beyond $2R$. The radial 2³S column is
$1.6\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$, and the λ10830 Sobolev depth is about 0.01 outside $2R$. The line comes out in weak
emission (EW −9 Å), with no absorption. Tripling the recombination rate into 2³S, or halving its photoionization
cross-section, raises the column to $3$–$5\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$ and still gives emission **[computed]**.

In the cooler star the 2³S level is photoionized 20 to 35 times more slowly, and the column is 23 times larger
(part of it in the hot gas at the shock). The line is still in emission **[computed]**.

LRDs show He I λ10830 absorption (@sec-lrd). In this model the far UV that ionizes hydrogen does not reach helium,
so λ10830 absorption needs a source of helium-ionizing photons that the model lacks: hotter gas, an accretion source,
or metal-line opacity changing the photosphere **[interpretation]**. This is a clear discriminant. A fed quasi-star
with only stellar and shock radiation should not absorb in λ10830.

### O I λ8446

Our gas has no metals. To estimate O I λ8446, pumped by Lyβ through the O I λ1025.77 line [@bowen1947], we use the
solution's Lyβ field with oxygen added as a trace (`julia/oi_bowen.jl`). Lyβ is optically thick everywhere, so each
$n=3\to1$ decay is a scattering. The infall scatters $8.3\times10^{57}$ Lyβ photons per second, 2000 times its rate
of Hα photons. O I absorbs a fraction $p = (O/H)(f_{\rm O}/f_{\rm Ly\beta}) \times$ overlap of these flights, and
each absorption yields one λ8446 photon.

- *Inputs.* Solar O/H $= 4.9\times10^{-4}$, an O I oscillator strength $f_{\rm O} = 0.01$ (a parameter, since we
  could not verify the value; the result scales linearly with it), and a line overlap of 0.5.
- *Result.* $p = 3\times10^{-5}$, giving $L(\lambda8446) \approx 6\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$, or 0.06 Hα photons'
  worth **[estimate]**.

This is an upper limit in spirit: it ignores the competition with Lyβ destruction and O I's other channels. It shows
that the Lyβ trapped in the infall is ample to make O I λ8446 strong if the gas has metals.

## What the tests say {#sec-tests-summary}

| question | result | status |
|---|---|---|
| Do the infall's electrons make the observed wings? | They make exponential wings of the observed width (exponential FWHM ≈ 1400 km s$^{-1}$, 17 % of Hα beyond 1000 km s$^{-1}$), but only on the blue side. A converging flow cannot make symmetric wings. | **[computed]** |
| Can outflow fix the symmetry? | Polar outflow over about half the sky ($\theta_o \approx 60°$) makes the wings symmetric at every inclination. Wider cones also make most absorbers blueshifted, as observed. The outflow is kinematic, not computed. | **[computed]**, model assumption |
| Is the Balmer break observable? | Yes. With the full series the observers' ratio is 3.6–4.3 (3.4 at $R = 100$), within the LRD range and set by the merging high Balmer lines of the infall's $n=2$ gas. | **[computed]**, bracket |
| What does a cooler star change? | At 5890 K the far UV is 3 to 40 times weaker, the infall stays mostly neutral and Hα is five times weaker. The decrement (7.9), Paβ/Hα and a strong redshifted Hα absorber move towards the data; $L_{\rm bol}/L({\rm H\alpha})$ moves away. | **[computed]**, energy deficit noted |
| Helium and oxygen? | No λ10830 absorption in either star: there are too few helium-ionizing photons. Lyβ trapping is ample for strong O I λ8446 if metals are present. | **[computed]**, **[estimate]** |

: The five tests in brief. {#tbl-tests-summary}

Taken together: a fed quasi-star reproduces the Balmer break and, given an outflow, the line wings and most absorbers. Its
Hα strength and its temperature pull in opposite directions between our two stars. It fails on He I λ10830, which
needs ionizing photons that neither the star nor the shock supply. The next decisive step is a two-dimensional
radiation-hydrodynamics run with inflow and outflow. Metals in the photosphere would also change the far UV, which
controls everything here **[interpretation]**.
